name: Surgical orthodontics

lead: Surgical orthodontics combines braces with corrective jaw surgery to fix bite problems, airway issues and facial imbalance, including receding chins, underbites, overbites and asymmetry. Appearance is among the stated goals, and the jaw position and profile change visibly.

Orthodontists align the teeth, and an oral and maxillofacial surgeon cuts and repositions the upper jaw, lower jaw or chin, usually through the mouth, fixing it with plates and screws. Studies report high post-surgical satisfaction, alongside depressive reactions during recovery in some patients.

paras: Treatment is coordinated between an orthodontist and a surgeon, and some patients have surgery before braces. Initial healing takes 2 to 6 weeks and bone union a further 2 to 4 months. The term is also used for surgically facilitated orthodontics, such as corticotomy, which aims to speed tooth movement.
Reported risks include bleeding, swelling, infection and facial numbness from nerve injury, which usually recovers within about three months. It is major surgery with weeks to months of recovery.

chain: Jaw bone is cut and repositioned
angle.text: Looksmaxxers consider jaw surgery with braces to correct bite, airway and facial imbalance, including recessed or overlong jaws. The jaw bone is repositioned, so the change in jaw position and profile is visible afterward.

lead: Surgical orthodontics usually refers to orthodontic treatment combined with orthognathic (corrective jaw) surgery, in which a surgeon cuts, moves and realigns jaw bone to correct bite problems, airway issues and facial imbalance, typically through the mouth and in coordination with an orthodontist [1]. The term is also used for surgically facilitated orthodontics, such as corticotomy, which aims to speed tooth movement [2].

Indications include skeletal jaw discrepancies, underbites, overbites, open bites, receding chins, sleep apnea, temporomandibular joint problems and facial asymmetry [1]. Appearance is among the stated goals, and surgery can improve facial aesthetics and self-esteem according to Wikipedia's summary [1].

Risks include bleeding, swelling, infection and facial numbness from nerve injury, which is usually temporary [1]. Psychological studies from the 1980s reported depressive reactions in some patients during recovery, alongside high satisfaction later [3][4].

paras: Bilateral sagittal split osteotomy corrects mandibular retrusion and prognathism by splitting and repositioning the lower jaw, fixed with plates and screws [1]. Genioplasty moves the chin, and maxillary (Le Fort-type) osteotomies address conditions such as vertical maxillary excess [1].

Conventional treatment uses braces for up to a year before surgery; surgery-first approaches and clear aligners are newer alternatives, and a surgery-first approach for mandibular prognathism has been described in a case report [1][5]. Virtual setups and software are used to plan and predict results [1][6].
An early published case was by Simon Hullihen in 1849, jaw osteotomies date to the 1940s, and Hugo Obwegeser popularised the sagittal split [1].

Reported risks include bleeding, swelling, infection (up to 7% in one summary), nausea and facial numbness, usually recovering within about three months [1]. Studies of emotional impact found depressive reactions in some surgical patients during the fixation-removal stage and up to nine months later [3][4].

A 9-month longitudinal study of 55 patients found satisfaction, self-esteem and body image high after surgery [3]. A follow-up study compared 90 surgical patients with 66 who considered surgery but chose conventional orthodontics, measuring mood states [4]. A review of orthodontic treatment and quality of life reports that patients seek treatment largely for appearance and social acceptance [7]. Registered trials examine surgically facilitated orthodontics: corticotomy effects on tooth movement (completed, 10 participants), piezoelectric decortication in adults (completed, 20), and acceleration of lower crowding (completed, 38) [2][8][9]. A randomised trial of surgically facilitated orthodontic treatment was withdrawn [10].
A 2017 study of YouTube videos on orthognathic surgery examined the quality of video content available to patients [11].

timeline.event: Simon Hullihen publishes an early jaw-surgery case.[1]
